title: How a Start-Up's Legal Bills Led to Spellbook, an AI Co-Pilot for Transactional Lawyers (Scott Stevenson - Co-Founder)
author: Scott Stevenson

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence
st.an: The source discusses only an anecdotal rationale for Spellbook’s branding and hoped-for resonance with fantasy-reading lawyers. It provides no position or evidence on pragmatic AI adoption, experimentation, organisational implementation, autonomous workflows or demonstrated transformation.
qs: So like we thought that there might be a little bit of a resonance there.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Stevenson accepts the cluster’s human-led copilot model and materially extends its workflow-redesign proposition with a concrete deployment principle: embed AI in lawyers’ existing tools rather than force a replacement interface. Rally’s adoption difficulties and his emphasis on sustained usage also add a behavioural measure of whether workflow integration is succeeding, while Spellbook’s claimed data controls add implementation detail on security.
qs: We just saw how hard it was to change the habits, and people just didn't want to go to yet another app.
They don't want to radically stop using Microsoft Word or go into some word replacement, which a lot of tech companies have tried to build.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Spellbook directly exemplifies the cluster’s principal proposition: a specialist legal workflow layer embedded in Microsoft Word that assists transactional lawyers with drafting and review while expressly retaining the lawyer rather than pursuing replacement. Its cross-application AI forecast is consistent with emerging agentic workflows, but remains predictive and does not establish autonomous legal-service performance or comparative product value.
qs: So Spellbook was our generative AI co-pilot for transactional lawyers and built right into Microsoft Word.
But we also never wanted to feel like it's replacing the lawyer because that's really not what we're about.

st.t: Technology delivery: Routine relief creates strategic capacity
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of technology as an integrated copilot for routine drafting and review, while appropriately stopping short of claiming measured performance or proven strategic-capacity gains. Its separate Percipient promotion also aligns with technology-supported service delivery but remains promotional rather than independent evidence.
qs: So Spellbook was our generative AI co-pilot for transactional lawyers and built right into Microsoft Word.
It can help you draft new clauses for agreements, review and find issues in your agreements and things like that.

kp.k: Startup legal costs motivated transactional automation
kp.d: Stevenson says legal bills for establishing Mune, basic IP work and a design patent consumed half its bank balance after a small angel investment. This personal experience motivated his pursuit of more affordable corporate and transactional legal work, rather than providing systematic evidence about legal costs.
qs: Before we knew it, we actually had a bill, legal bills added up to half of the money in our bank account.
It was like, people should just be able to start a company and protect their IP for reasonable amounts of money.

kp.k: Bespoke transactions limited template automation adoption
kp.d: Stevenson reports selling Rally to 200 law firms but describes lengthy precedent collection and template setup, sometimes taking a year, followed by customers finding their work too bespoke. He distinguishes law firms' varied clients and documents from in-house teams' potentially greater standardisation opportunities and explicitly retracts his early belief that templates could eliminate lawyers.
qs: We sold that technology to 200 law firms.
I was like, no one will need lawyers anywhere after this. We were dead wrong on that.
Maybe if you're in an in-house team, you can really standardize things really well, or in your case you work with a lot of in-house teams.
Then they'd be like, you know what, this is awesome, but my work is a little bit too bespoke.

kp.k: Generative AI shifted Rally's product direction
kp.d: Stevenson says Spellbook began as a lead-generation side project for Rally and launched in summer 2022 as a transactional-law copilot inside Microsoft Word. An initial GPT-2 version was not fully released because results were inadequate; GPT-3 improved results enough to launch. His claim to have preceded other generative legal products is qualified by his own awareness of the market.
qs: We thought it would just get us some attention and get some leads, and it would just be a little side project.
So the very first version was built on GPT-2. They were not quite there, so we didn't fully push that out.
But as soon as GPT-3 was available, we started getting much better results and then we pushed it out.
Yeah, we pushed this out before ChatGPT, really before any other generative AI legal product that I've come across.
It was summer of 2022, so it was still close when it was fully launched.

kp.k: Contract drafting and review remain lawyer-controlled
kp.d: Stevenson describes clause retrieval, clause generation, instruction-driven contract review and rewriting selected text for tone or negotiating posture. Spellbook proposes document-wide redlines using Word's tracked changes, which the lawyer must accept. These are vendor descriptions of augmentation capabilities, not measured productivity or accuracy findings.
qs: We can help you find that clause or language from past language you drafted or we can generate a clause that can fit an agreement to meet your specs.

Spellbook will take that instruction and actually redline the whole document using track changes in Word to actually make a whole bunch of concrete suggestions throughout your document about what language you might want to push for or modify.
You got to accept changes. Yeah, but it will give you those direct suggestions of you should change X, change Y, change Z.

kp.k: Playbooks and clause libraries encode repeatable preferences
kp.d: Stevenson says users can save review instructions as playbooks, including conditional instructions for specialised language, and connect previous documents to a Clause Library that surfaces reusable clauses. He distinguishes these existing features from a beta policies feature, expected over the next month or so, intended to check agreements against recurring requirements and score passing or failing checks.
qs: you can actually save a set of instructions that you can then run again and again against your agreements.
We also have something called our Clause Library, where you can actually connect all of the previous docs that you've drafted or work with
You could write that as an instruction in your Playbook to say, if you see X, then do Y.
The Playbooks are really geared towards redlining a document and making changes. Our policies are more of a quick check, and this is something we're just about to roll out over the next month or so.

kp.d: Drawing on Rally's separate web application, Stevenson argues that favourable user feedback can conceal failure to change working habits. He treats continued usage three months after purchase as more revealing and explains Word integration as a way to enhance lawyers' established workflow rather than require replacement tools. He presents application fatigue as a wider software problem, not exclusively a lawyer characteristic.
qs: With the Rally product, we built our whole web application where we'd take lawyers out of their normal workflow to our own UI.

But when you actually look at the usage patterns, like is this customer still using the product three months after they bought it? That's where you see the truth of, are people able to actually change their habits?
In software as a whole, people are sick of jumping between so many different apps.
our whole company is based around the idea of lawyers know how to ride a bicycle. Let's give them an electric bicycle.

kp.k: Confidentiality protections depend on storage and personalisation choices
kp.d: Stevenson asserts that users can opt out of all data storage, with encrypted transmission and no data retained by Spellbook. For customers choosing learning, training or clause storage, he claims de-identification removes sensitive information and PII. These are the vendor's stated protections; the discussion supplies no independent security findings.
qs: But you can completely opt out of any data storage whatsoever.
So all that happens is your data gets encrypted, goes over the wire, we get a response back and it's fed to you and no data is kept or stored by us.
we can fully de-identify the data and remove key, sensitive information and PII from anything that is kept or used for training.

kp.k: Desktop-controlling AI could extend automation across applications
kp.d: Stevenson predicts that AI capable of controlling a desktop mouse and moving between applications will enter legal-tech products within two years of the conversation. His example combines drafting an email response with downloading and processing a client attachment. He agrees with the host that native application interaction could obviate some APIs; this is a forecast, not a demonstrated Spellbook capability.
qs: now people are toying with AI that actually controls the mouse on your desktop and moves between multiple applications and stuff like that.
That's something that I think is within two years, we're going to now see that in probably legal tech products
help me draft a response to this client and also download their attachment and do X, Y, and Z to it and AI will actually go and do those things.
This means AI will be able to access pretty much anything that runs on your computer very soon.

kp.k: Reported growth prompted further investment and organisational expansion
kp.d: Stevenson reports 10x growth in onboarded lawyers last year, reaching around 1,700 law firms and in-house legal teams, and around 500 prospective-customer meetings per week. He describes raising a first 10 million in early 2022 and 20 million US about a year later, with existing investor Inovia seeking to accelerate growth. He links the capital to product development and expanding support, customer success and sales. These are self-reported figures with the transcript's relative timing.
qs: Early 2022, we raised our first 10 million, and then about a year later now we have just raised 20 million US.
We grew 10x in terms of the number of lawyers that were on board last year
we just had incredible growth last year, going to around 1,700 law firms and in-house legal teams.
we're currently booking around 500 meetings per week with prospective customers.

kp.k: Development priorities include accuracy, personalisation and broader workflows
kp.d: Stevenson identifies resistance to hallucination, improved accuracy, learning users' drafting preferences and language, and expansion beyond Word as investment priorities. The envisaged broader workflow begins with a client email and attachment and helps coordinate the response and review. These are development commitments and aspirations, without reported error rates or validation results.
qs: it's making these things more accurate and very resistant to any kind of hallucination that's always on everyone's mind.
So enabling the systems to learn your style and preferences over time as you're working and to use your language and to do things your way is another important pillar for us.
And branching out beyond word to other workflows is something else that we're doing.

kp.k: Stevenson rejects lawyer replacement as Spellbook's purpose
kp.d: Explaining the product's positioning and name, Stevenson frames Spellbook as a tool or sidekick supporting lawyers, not an autonomous substitute. He expresses the belief that human lawyers will remain necessary for a very long time; this is a strategic position and prediction, not employment evidence.
qs: But we also never wanted to feel like it's replacing the lawyer because that's really not what we're about.
we actually are strongly in the camp that human lawyers are going to be very needed for a very long time.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Scott Stevenson presents AI as a transactional lawyer's drafting and review assistant, predicts cross-application automation, and expects human lawyers to remain necessary.
pts.d: Stevenson makes six principal claims. (1) Spellbook can generate contract clauses to specifications, retrieve previously used language, rewrite selected text, and redline whole agreements according to instructions, with lawyers accepting the suggested changes. (2) Saved playbooks and clause libraries support repeatable, practice-specific review; a forthcoming policies feature would check agreements against user-defined requirements and report passing or failing checks. (3) Embedding AI in Microsoft Word improves fit with lawyers' established workflows rather than requiring migration to another application. (4) Within two years of the interview, he expects legal-tech products to use AI that controls desktop applications, handling client emails and attachments across applications and reducing reliance on APIs. (5) He says further product development can improve accuracy and resistance to hallucination, learn lawyers' preferences, and extend assistance beyond Word; these are development priorities rather than reported measured improvements. (6) He explicitly rejects lawyer replacement as Spellbook's purpose and predicts continued need for human lawyers for a long time. Separately, he reports rapid commercial adoption and describes optional no-storage and de-identification arrangements as enabling use with sensitive client information.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists primarily of Stevenson's product descriptions, founder experience, self-reported adoption figures, and observations of emerging technology.
pts.d: For drafting, redlining, retrieval, playbooks and privacy, Stevenson describes the vendor's functionality and operating practices; the interview supplies no independent tests, accuracy benchmarks, quantified time savings or client-cost comparisons. For workflow integration and the limits of conventional automation, he draws on Rally's experience selling to 200 law firms: template setup could take a year, bespoke work limited usefulness, and customers struggled to change application habits despite positive initial feedback. He reports tenfold growth in onboarded lawyers in the preceding year and approximately 1,700 law-firm and in-house-team customers; these are adoption figures, not evidence of legal-work quality or productivity gains. His desktop-agent prediction rests on seeing experimental technology on Twitter/X and his belief that such experiments precede commercial products by about two years. Accuracy improvements and personalization are investment objectives, not demonstrated outcomes. Continued need for lawyers is expressed as a conviction, informed in the discussion by his earlier experience underestimating the complexity of legal work.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source distinguishes current assistance from near-term product releases, a two-year automation forecast, and an indefinite expectation of continued human involvement.
pts.d: Drafting, review, track-change suggestions, playbooks and clause retrieval are described as available at the time of the interview. Stevenson dates Spellbook's public launch to summer 2022, following an insufficiently capable GPT-2 prototype and better GPT-3 results. Policies are described as a beta feature expected to roll out in roughly a month. Desktop control in legal-tech products is predicted within two years, while broader access to desktop applications is described as coming 'very soon.' Personalization, accuracy work and expansion beyond Word have no precise completion dates. Human lawyers are expected to remain needed 'for a very long time,' without a numerical horizon. Assistance is conditional on lawyer instructions, relevant prior documents or configured playbooks, and human acceptance of redlines. Privacy claims distinguish opting out of storage from opting into storage or learning with de-identification. Growth figures refer to 'last year.' Although the document is labeled 2025, its internal funding chronology and relative dates do not establish a consistent interview date, so these relative horizons should not be converted into definite calendar-year predictions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected users are transactional lawyers in law firms and in-house teams; the proposed change is assisted contract work rather than autonomous legal representation.
pts.d: Law-firm transactional lawyers receive drafting and review suggestions inside Word, including support for bespoke deals and specialized language. In-house legal teams are also customers, although Stevenson distinguishes their potentially more standardized work from law firms' varied matters. Lawyers retain responsibility for deciding whether to accept proposed language; the source does not quantify the burden of verifying AI output. Clients are affected through lawyers' negotiation instructions, treatment of confidential documents, and prospective email-and-attachment workflows. His startup legal-bill experience motivates a desire for more affordable company formation and IP protection, but the interview does not establish that Spellbook achieves particular client savings or closes the access-to-justice gap. Spellbook is presented as a software vendor, not an alternative legal service provider delivering legal work. No concrete predictions are offered about associate staffing, partner leverage, billing models or legal-job losses.
